species.name: Abies amabilis
species.native_region: the Pacific Northwest of North America

species.name: Abies grandis
species.description: Needles were used for hair perfume (Nuxalk, Hesquiaht); boughs for purification (Kwakwaka’wakw); branches burned as incense, air freshener, protection against illness (Ditidaht); boughs rubbed on skin of girls for protection against predators, used as a protective wash (Nlaka’pamux) Boughs for bedding, flooring, incense; pitch for glue. (Boas 1921, 1966; H.I. Smith 1928; Turner 1973; Turner and Bell 1973; Turner and Efrat 1982; Turner, Thomas, et al. 1983, 1990).

species.name: Abies homolepis
species.native_region: the mountains of central and southern Honshū and Shikoku, Japan

species.name: Acer
species.description: This is a genus only identification, not species.

species.name: Acer campestre
species.native_region: Continental Europe, Britain, southwest Asia from Turkey to the Caucasus, and north Africa in the Atlas Mountains

species.name: Acer ginnala
species.native_region: northeastern Asia from easternmost Mongolia east to Korea and Japan, and north to the Russian Far East in the Amur River valley
species.description: It is a small maple with deciduous leaves that is sometimes grown as a garden subject or boulevard tree.

species.name: Acer macrophyllum
species.native_region: western North America, mostly near the Pacific coast, from southernmost Alaska to southern California
species.description: Indigenous peoples used bigleaf maple for canoe paddles, spindle whorls, bowls, dishes, masks, and clubs.

species.name: Acer palmatum
species.native_region: Japan, Korea, China, eastern Mongolia, and southeast Russia
species.description: Acer palmatum has been cultivated in Japan for centuries and in temperate areas around the world since the 1800s.

species.name: Acer platanoides
species.native_region: eastern and central Europe and western Asia, from France east to Russia, north to southern Scandinavia and southeast to northern Iran

species.name: Acer pseudoplatanus
species.native_region: Central Europe and Western Asia, from France eastwards to Ukraine, northern Turkey and the Caucasus and southwards in the mountains of northern Spain and Italy

species.name: Acer rubrum
species.native_region: Eastern and central North America

species.name: Aesculus × carnea
species.description: Artificial hybrid between A. pavia (red buckeye) and A. hippocastanum (horse-chestnut)

species.name: Aesculus hippocastanum
species.native_region: the Balkans, Southeast Europe
species.description:
The common name "horse-chestnut" (often unhyphenated) is reported as having originated from the erroneous belief that the tree was a kind of chestnut (though in fact only distantly related), together with the alleged observation that the fruit or seeds could help panting or coughing horses.

In Germany, horse-chestnuts are often found in beer gardens, particularly in Bavaria. Prior to the advent of mechanical refrigeration, brewers would dig cellars for lagering. To further protect the cellars from the summer heat, they would plant chestnut trees, which have spreading, dense canopies but shallow roots which would not intrude on the caverns. The practice of serving beer at these sites evolved into the modern beer garden.

species.name: Aesculus indica
species.native_region: the Himalayan Lowlands, between Kashmir and Western Nepal at elevations between 900 and 3,000 metres

species.name: Ailanthus altissima
species.native_region: both northeast and central China, as well as Taiwan
species.description:
In China, the tree of heaven has a long and rich history. It was mentioned in the oldest extant Chinese dictionary and listed in many Chinese medical texts for its purported curative ability.

It is considered a noxious weed and vigorous invasive species, and one of the worst invasive plant species in Europe and North America.

species.name: Alnus rubra
species.description:
Used by First Peoples for bowls and trays, masks, canoe bailers, paddles, firedrills. Cooking & smoking. Dye. Bark would be partially harvested for medicinal use, rectangular pieces cut from living trees.

In moist forest areas Alnus rubra will rapidly cover a former burn or clearcut, often preventing the establishment of conifers. It is a prolific seed producer, but the small, wind-dispersed seeds require an open area of mineral soil to germinate, and so skid trails and other areas disturbed by logging or fire are ideal seedbeds.

species.name: Amelanchier × grandiflora
species.description: A hybrid of garden origin between A. arborea and A. laevis.

species.name: Araucaria araucana
species.native_region: central and southern Chile and western Argentina
species.description:
Because of the prevalence of similar species in ancient prehistory, it is sometimes called a living fossil. It is also the national tree of Chile.

The origin of the popular English language name "monkey puzzle" derives from its early cultivation in Britain in about 1850, when the species was still very rare in gardens and not widely known. Sir William Molesworth, the owner of a young specimen at Pencarrow garden near Bodmin in Cornwall, was showing it to a group of friends, when one of them – the noted barrister and Benthamist Charles Austin – remarked, "It would puzzle a monkey to climb that".

Its piñones, or seeds, are edible, similar to large pine nuts, and are harvested by indigenous peoples in Argentina and Chile.

species.name: Arbutus menziesii
species.native_region: the western coastal areas of North America, from British Columbia to California
species.description:
Many mammal and bird species feed off the berries. The berries dry up and have hooked barbs that latch onto larger animals for migration.

Although drought tolerant and relatively fast growing, Arbutus menziesii is currently declining throughout most of its range. One likely cause is fire control; under natural conditions, the madrona depends on intermittent naturally occurring fires to reduce the conifer overstory. Mature trees survive fire, and can regenerate more rapidly after fire than the Douglas firs with which they are often associated. They also produce very large numbers of seeds, which sprout following fire.

Indigenous peoples ate the berries raw and cooked, but because the berries have a high tannin content and are thus astringent, they more often chewed them or made them into a cider. They also used the berries to make necklaces and other decorations, and as bait for fishing. Bark and leaves were used to treat stomach aches, cramps, skin ailments, and sore throats. The bark was often made into a tea to be drunk for these medicinal purposes. Wood was spared as fuel and for any other use by Saanich for spiritual reasons (because of its service to people during the Great Flood).

species.name: Austrocedrus chilensis
species.native_region: the Valdivian temperate rain forests and the adjacent drier steppe-forests of central-southern Chile and western Argentina

species.name: Betula nigra
species.native_region: the Eastern United States

species.name: Betula papyrifera
species.description:
Indigenous peoples used the bark for baskets, lining cache pits, burials, etc. It would be removed from standing, living trees without killing the tree (general, Tsilhqot’in, Ulkatcho Dakelth, Dene [Athabaskan], Secwepemc, Okanagan, Ktunaxa)

Betula papyrifera is a pioneer species, meaning it is often one of the first trees to grow in an area after other trees are removed by some sort of disturbance. Typical disturbances colonized by paper birch are wildfire, avalanche, or windthrow areas where the wind has blown down all trees. When it grows in these pioneer, or early successional, woodlands, it often forms stands of trees where it is the only species.

species.name: Betula pendula
species.native_region: Europe and parts of Asia

species.name: Betula populifolia
species.native_region: eastern North America

species.name: Calocedrus decurrens
species.native_region: western North America

species.name: Carpinus betulus
species.native_region: Western Asia and central, eastern, and southern Europe, including southern England

species.name: Castanea sativa
species.native_region: Southern Europe and Asia Minor
species.description: A substantial, long-lived deciduous tree, it produces an edible seed, the chestnut, which has been used in cooking since ancient times.

species.name: Cedrus atlantica
species.native_region: Atlas Mountains of Morocco (Middle Atlas, High Atlas), to the Rif, and to the Tell Atlas in Algeria
species.description: C. atlantica is common in cultivation as an ornamental tree in temperate climates. In garden settings, often the glaucous (bluish green) forms are planted as ornamental trees, distinguished as the Glauca group, a cultivar group.

species.name: Cedrus deodara
species.native_region: western Himalayas in Eastern Afghanistan, Northern Pakistan and India, Southwestern Tibet and Western Nepal
species.description: The botanical name, which is also the English common name, derives from the Sanskrit term devadāru, which means "wood of the gods", a compound of deva "god" and dāru "wood and tree". Among Hindus, as the etymology of deodar suggests, it is worshiped as a divine tree.

species.name: Cedrus libani
species.native_region: mountains of the Eastern Mediterranean basin
species.description: It is a large evergreen conifer that has great religious and historical significance in the cultures of the Middle East, and is referenced many times in the literature of ancient civilisations. It is the national emblem of Lebanon and is widely used as an ornamental tree in parks and gardens.

species.name: Cercidiphyllum japonicum
species.native_region: Japan
species.description: The Katsura tree is sometimes called caramel tree for the light caramel smell it emits during leaf fall.

species.name: Chamaecyparis lawsoniana
species.native_region: Oregon and northwestern California

species.name: Chamaecyparis obtusa
species.native_region: Japan
species.description: It is grown for its very high quality timber in Japan, where it is used as a material for building palaces, temples, shrines, traditional noh theatres, baths, table tennis blades and masu.

species.name: Chamaecyparis pisifera
species.native_region: central and southern Japan, on the islands of Honshū and Kyūshū

species.name: Cladrastis kentukea
species.native_region: the Southeastern United States, with a restricted range from western North Carolina west to eastern Oklahoma, and from southern Missouri and Indiana south to central Alabama

species.name: Cornus
species.description: This is a genus-only identification.

species.name: Cornus florida
species.native_region: eastern North America and northern Mexico

species.name: Cornus kousa
species.native_region: East Asia including Korea, China and Japan

species.name: Cornus nuttallii
species.native_region: western North America from the lowlands of southern British Columbia to the mountains of southern California, with an inland population in central Idaho
species.description:
This deciduous, flowering tree has been used for many purposes by indigenous communities from the west coast of British Columbia to California. The wood was used to make harpoons, bow, arrows, combs, and needle hooks. The Cowichan people on Vancouver Island made knitting needles from the Pacific Dogwood. The Straits Salish used the bark to make dark brown or red dye. The bark was also used medicinally to treat skin infections, fevers, digestive issues, to purify the blood to strengthen the lungs, and as an antiseptic. In 1956 the Pacific Dogwood was adopted as British Columbia’s floral emblem.

Cornus nuttallii is named after Thomas Nuttall, an English botanist and zoologist who worked in North America in the nineteenth century.

species.name: Crataegus × grignonensis
species.native_region: Arboretum de Grignon, France

species.name: Crataegus × lavalleei
species.description: The female parent was C. mexicana (sometimes mistakenly called C. pubescens), and the male parent is thought to be C. calpodendron.

species.name: Crataegus crus-galli
species.native_region: eastern North America from Ontario to Texas to Florida

species.name: Crataegus douglasii
species.native_region: northern and western North America
species.description:
Hard wood used by First Peoples for digging sticks, hammers, and implement handles.

It is named after David Douglas, who collected seed from the plant during his botanical explorations.

species.name: Crataegus laevigata
species.native_region: western and central Europe, from Great Britain (where it is largely confined to lowland ancient woodland) and Spain east to the Czech Republic and Hungary.

species.name: Crataegus oxyacantha
species.native_region: Northern Europe
species.description: The name Crataegus oxyacantha L. has been rejected as being of uncertain application, but is sometimes still used. Likely the same as Crataegus monogyna

species.name: Cryptomeria japonica
species.native_region: China, Japan
species.description: Sugi is the national tree of Japan, commonly planted around temples and shrines, with many hugely impressive trees planted centuries ago.

species.name: Cunninghamia lanceolata
species.native_region: China, northern Vietnam and Laos, and perhaps also Cambodia
species.description:
The genus name Cunninghamia honours Dr. James Cunningham, a British doctor who introduced this species into cultivation in 1702 and botanist Allan Cunningham.

Cunninghamia is a prized timber tree in China, producing soft, highly durable scented wood similar to that of Coast Redwood and Sugi. It is used in particular for manufacture of coffins and in temple building where the scent is valued.

species.name: Cupressus
species.description: These trees haven't been fully identified.

species.name: Cupressus × leylandii
species.native_region: Wales
species.description:
In 1888 at Leighton Hall, an estate in Wales, the hybrid cross occurred when the female flowers or cones of Yellow cedar were fertilised by pollen from Monterey cypress in gardens owned by Liverpool banker Christopher Leyland.

In 1925, a firm of commercial nurserymen specialising in conifers were looking for a breed which was fast-growing, and could be deployed in hard-to-grow windy and salty areas such as Cornwall. Eventually they found the six original trees developed by Leyland, and began propagating the species. Commercial nurseries spotted the plant’s potential, and for many years it was the biggest-selling item in every garden centre in Great Britain, making up to 10% of their total sales.

species.name: Cupressus arizonica
species.native_region: the southwestern United States (Arizona, Utah, southwestern New Mexico, and southern California, with a few populations in southern Nevada and in the Chisos Mountains of western Texas), and in Mexico (Coahuila, Nuevo León, Chihuahua, Sonora, Durango, Tamaulipas, Zacatecas and northern Baja California)

species.name: Cupressus cashmeriana
species.native_region: the eastern Himalaya in Bhutan and adjacent areas of Arunachal Pradesh in northeastern India
species.description: It is the official national tree of Bhutan, where it is often associated with Buddhist religious places. It has been widely planted around Vihara monasteries and Buddhist temples there for centuries.

species.name: Cupressus nootkatensis
species.native_region: coastal regions of northwestern North America
species.description:
The specific epithet "nootkatensis" is derived from its discovery by Europeans on the lands of a First Nation of Canada, those lands of the Nuu-chah-nulth people of Vancouver Island, British Columbia, who were formerly referred to as the Nootka.

The Nootka cypress is used extensively by the indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast, along with another cypress, Thuja plicata (western red cedar). While western red cedar was preferred for larger projects (houses, canoes), Nootka cypress was used for smaller carvings such as vessels and utensils. Boughs are used in sweat bath, as scrubbers, for rheumatism, arthritis, and protection (Kwakwaka’wakw) (Boas 1930; Turner and Bell 1973). Used for bows, canoe paddles, carving. Inner bark used for baskets, mats, clothing, blankets. Bark harvested for weaving material; only partially harvested so as not to kill tree (widely, Northwest Coast).

This species has been considered to be one of the finest timber trees in the world and has been exported to China during the last century. The wood has been used for flooring, interior finish and shipbuilding.

species.name: Fagus sylvatica
species.native_region: Europe

species.name: Fraxinus angustifolia
species.native_region: central and southern Europe, northwest Africa, and southwest Asia

species.name: Fraxinus ornus
species.native_region: Southern Europe and southwestern Asia, from Spain and Italy north to Austria, Poland and the Czech Republic, and east through the Balkans, Turkey, and western Syria to Lebanon and Armenia
species.description: A sugary extract from the sap may be obtained by making a cut in the bark; this was compared in late medieval times (attested by around 1400 AD) with the biblical manna, giving rise to the English name of the tree, and some of the vernacular names from its native area (fresno del maná in Spanish, frassino da manna in Italian). In fact, the sugar mannose and the sugar alcohol mannitol both derive their names from the extract.

species.name: Fraxinus pennsylvanica
species.native_region: eastern and central North America, from Nova Scotia west to southeastern Alberta and eastern Colorado, south to northern Florida, and southwest to Oklahoma and eastern Texas

species.name: Ginkgo biloba
species.native_region: China
species.description: The ginkgo is classified in its own division, the Ginkgophyta, comprising the single class Ginkgoopsida, order Ginkgoales, family Ginkgoaceae, genus Ginkgo and is the only extant species within this group. It is one of the best-known examples of a living fossil, because Ginkgoales other than G. biloba are not known from the fossil record after the Pliocene.

species.name: Gleditsia triacanthos
species.native_region: central North America
species.description: Honey locust is highly adaptable to different environments, has been introduced worldwide, and is an aggressive invasive species.

species.name: Gleditsia triacanthos var. inermis
species.native_region: central North America
species.description: Honey locust is highly adaptable to different environments, has been introduced worldwide, and is an aggressive invasive species. var. inermis is the thornless form.

species.name: Hesperocyparis macrocarpa
species.native_region: the Central Coast of California
species.description: Because of the large trunk size some trees develop, people have assumed that individual H. macrocarpa trees may be up to 2,000 years old. However, the longest-lived report based on physical evidence is only 284 years old. The renowned Californian botanist Willis Linn Jepson wrote that "the advertisement of [C. macrocarpa trees] in seaside literature as 1,000 to 2,000 years old does not ... rest upon any actual data, and probably represents a desire to minister to a popular craving for superlatives".

species.name: Ilex aquifolium
species.native_region: western and southern Europe, northwest Africa, and southwest Asia

species.name: Juglans regia
species.native_region: the region stretching from the Balkans eastward to the Himalayas and southwest China
species.description: In the fourth century BC, Alexander the Great introduced this "Persian nut" in Macedonian and Greek ancestral forms with lateral fruiting from Iran and Central Asia.

species.name: Juniperus chinensis
species.native_region: China, Taiwan, Myanmar, Japan, Korea and the Russian Far East

species.name: Juniperus virginiana
species.native_region: eastern North America from southeastern Canada to the Gulf of Mexico and east of the Great Plains.

species.name: Koelreuteria bipinnata
species.native_region: southern China
species.description: It is one of the few trees that bloom in summer.

species.name: Laburnum × watereri
species.native_region: Central Europe
species.description: A naturally occurring hybrid, its parents are common laburnum, Laburnum anagyroides, and alpine laburnum, Laburnum alpinum.

species.name: Larix decidua
species.native_region: the mountains of central Europe

species.name: Liquidambar styraciflua
species.native_region: warm temperate areas of eastern North America and tropical montane regions of Mexico and Central America
species.description: Sweetgum is one of the most important commercial hardwoods in the Southeastern United States. It is also a popular ornamental and forestal tree, cultivated for its distinctive foliage and intense autumn colors.

species.name: Liriodendron tulipifera
species.native_region: eastern North America from Southern Ontario and possibly southern Quebec to Illinois eastward to southwestern Massachusetts and Rhode Island, and south to central Florida and Louisiana
species.description:
The tulip tree is the tallest eastern hardwood.

This tree species is a major honey plant in the eastern United States, yielding a dark reddish, fairly strong honey which gets mixed reviews as a table honey but is favorably regarded by bakers; nectar is produced in the orange part of the flowers.

The tulip tree has been referenced in many poems and the namesakes of other poems, such as William Stafford's "Tulip Tree." It is also a plot element in the Edgar Allan Poe short story "The Gold-Bug".

species.name: Magnolia × 'Galaxy'
species.description: Magnolia 'Galaxy' is the result of a cross between Magnolia liliiflora and Magnolia sprengeri 'Diva'.

species.name: Magnolia × soulangeana
species.description: Magnolia × soulangeana was initially bred by French plantsman Étienne Soulange-Bodin (1774–1846), a retired cavalry officer in Napoleon's army, at his château de Fromont near Paris. He crossed Magnolia denudata with M. liliiflora in 1820, and was impressed with the resulting progeny's first precocious flowering in 1826.

species.name: Magnolia grandiflora
species.native_region: the southeastern United States
species.description:
Squirrels, opossums, quail, and turkey are known to eat the seeds.

Over 150 cultivars have been developed and named, although only 30 to 40 of these still exist and still fewer are commercially propagated and sold.

species.name: Magnolia kobus
species.native_region: Japan (Kyushu, Honshu, and Hokkaido) and Korea

species.name: Malus × purpurea
species.description: This crab was raised by Messrs Barbier of Orleans around 1900 by crossing M. niedzwetzkyana with M. × atrosanguinea (M. floribunda atrosanguinea)

species.name: Malus × zumi
species.native_region: Japan
species.description: Introduced to N. America in 1892 by Sargent, and thence to Kew in 1905.

species.name: Malus sylvestris
species.native_region: Europe

species.name: Metasequoia glyptostroboides
species.native_region: The border region of Hubei and Hunan provinces and Chongqing municipality in south-central China
species.description: This species was known only from fossils and thought to be extinct, until its rediscovery in China in 1944.

species.name: Nyssa sylvatica
species.native_region: eastern North America from the coastal Northeastern United States and southern Ontario south to central Florida and eastern Texas, as well as Mexico

species.name: Parrotia persica
species.native_region: northern Iran and southern Azerbaijan

species.name: Picea abies
species.native_region: Northern, Central and Eastern Europe
species.description: The Norway spruce is one of the most widely planted spruces, both in and outside of its native range, and one of the most economically important coniferous species in Europe.

species.name: Picea glauca
species.native_region: central Alaska all through the east, across southern/central Canada to the Avalon Peninsula in Newfoundland

species.name: Picea omorika
species.native_region: the Drina River valley in western Serbia, and eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina
species.description: It has a total range of only about 60 ha. Outside its native range, Serbian spruce is of major importance as an ornamental tree in large gardens, valued in northern Europe and North America for its very attractive crown form and ability to grow on a wide range of soils

species.name: Picea pungens
species.native_region: North America
species.description: The blue spruce is the State Tree of Colorado.

species.name: Picea sitchensis
species.description:
Said to bring supernatural protection (Haida, Kwakwaka’wakw, Klallam, Ditidaht); bark mixture in sweat bath, decoction drunk for tuberculosis (Nuxalk); branches placed around sick people’s houses with the idea that the sharp spruce needles would keep anything unclean from entering the house; spruce tips rubbed on canoes, digging sticks, and implements to purify them and used to cleanse a person contaminated (sic) with menstrual blood (Kwakwaka’wakw); beating with branches said to drive away the sickness and ghosts of the dead (Klallam); said to bring vivid dreams and good luck if you sleep under spruce (Nlaka’pamux) (Boas 1930, 1966; Turner 2004a; Turner, Thomas, et al. 1983). 

Wood used for bows, wedges, blanket pins, arrows and arrow points, tongs, clubs, implement handles,
ladders, drying racks, hollowed out containers, fish traps, deadfalls, shelters. Roots for twined basketry, fishing lines, snares, binding and tying; bark sheets for roofing. Pitch for sealing canoes and
baskets, waterproofing, glue.

Pitch or gum harvested from living trees for material or medicinal purposes. Collected from natural or human-made wounds in trees or from pitch blisters. The pitch was variously chewed for pleasure, used as waterproofing or adhesive for implements and containers, or prepared for medicinal use.         -- Roots harvested for basketry; only a few taken from a single tree in any one year; limbs and sapling trunks used for fish weirs; inner bark (food) and pitch (medicine, adhesive) harvested from individual living trees over generations (Haida, Tlingit, Ts’msyen, Kwakwaka’wakw, other Northwest
Coast peoples).

species.name: Pinus
species.description: This is a genus only identification, not species.

species.name: Pinus contorta
species.native_region: western North America
species.description: Pinus contorta is a fire-dependent species, requiring wildfires to maintain healthy populations of diverse ages. The bark of the lodgepole pine is fairly thin, minimizing the tree's defense to fire; however, the heat of fire opens the cones to release the seeds. This allows the species to regenerate and maintain its place in the forest habitat.

species.name: Pinus coulteri
species.native_region: the coastal mountains of Southern California and northern Baja California (Mexico)
species.description: The outstanding characteristic of this tree is the large, spiny cones which are 20–40 cm (7.9–15.7 in) long, and weigh 2–5 kg (4.4–11.0 lb) when fresh. Coulter pines produce the largest cones of any pine tree species (people are actually advised to wear hardhats when working in Coulter pine groves), although the slender cones of the sugar pine are longer. The large size of the cones has earned them the nickname "widowmakers" among locals.

species.name: Pinus jeffreyi
species.native_region: California, also in the westernmost part of Nevada, southwestern Oregon, and northern Baja California
species.description:
The scent of Pinus jeffreyi is variously described as reminiscent of vanilla, lemon, pineapple, violets, apple, and, quite commonly, butterscotch; This scent may be sampled by breaking off a shoot or some needles, or by simply smelling the resin's scent in between the plates of the bark.

The exceptional purity of n-heptane distilled from Pinus jeffreyi resin led to n-heptane being selected as the zero point on the octane rating scale of petrol. 

Pinus jeffreyi is closely related to Pinus ponderosa (ponderosa pine) and is similar in appearance. One way to distinguish between them is by their cones. Each has barbs at the end of the scales. The sharp Pinus jeffreyi cone scale barbs point inward, so the cone feels smooth to the palm of one's hand when rubbed down the cone. Pinus ponderosa cone scale barbs point outward, so feel sharp and prickly to the palm of one's hands. This gives rise to the memory device for distinguishing between them - "gentle Jeffrey and prickly ponderosa".

species.name: Pinus monticola
species.native_region: the mountains of the western United States and Canada, specifically the Sierra Nevada, the Cascade Range, the Coast Range, and the northern Rocky Mountains
species.description: Sheets of bark harvested for baskets and canoes from living trees (Ktunaxa, Lakes, Secwepemc)

species.name: Pinus mugo
species.native_region: high elevation habitats from southwestern to Central Europe and Southeast Europe

species.name: Pinus nigra
species.native_region: Turkey, Southern Italy, Morocco, Algeria

species.name: Pinus pinaster
species.native_region: Western Mediterranean
species.description: Tree A296 has been misidentified by others as the Allepo Pine, Pinus halepensis. For details of identification see: https://naturevictoria.com/species/p-pinaster.html

species.name: Pinus ponderosa
species.native_region: Mountainous regions of western North America

species.name: Pinus sabiniana
species.native_region: California

species.name: Pinus sylvestris
species.native_region: Eurasia, ranging from Western Europe to Eastern Siberia, south to the Caucasus Mountains and Anatolia, and north to well inside the Arctic Circle in Fennoscandia.
species.description:
Scots pine was one of the first trees introduced to North America, in about 1600.

It has been widely used in the United States for the Christmas tree trade, and was one of the most popular Christmas trees from the 1950s through the 1980s.

The Scots pine was grown and used extensively in the coal mining regions of Flanders, Belgium. It was used to fortify the tunnelling and preferred for its cracking sound when in need of replacing. Large patches of forest containing mostly this species are still scattered over the countryside.

species.name: Pinus thunbergiana
species.native_region: coastal areas of Japan (Kyūshū, Shikoku and Honshū) and South Korea

species.name: Platanus × acerifolia
species.description: The London plane is usually thought to be a hybrid of Platanus orientalis (oriental plane) and Platanus occidentalis (American sycamore). The species was formed by hybridization in the 17th century after P. orientalis and P. occidentalis had been planted in proximity to one another. It is often said that the hybridization took place in Spain, but it could also have happened in Vauxhall Gardens in London where John Tradescant the Younger discovered the tree in the mid-17th century.

species.name: Platycladus orientalis
species.native_region: northeastern parts of eastern Asia and north Asia
species.description:
The wood is used in Buddhist temples both for construction work, and chipped, for incense burning.

Platycladus was often included in Thuja, which is reflected in one of its common names, "oriental thuja". But it is only distantly related to the genus Thuja. Differences include its distinct cones, wingless seeds, and its almost scentless foliage.

species.name: Populus nigra
species.native_region: Europe, southwest and central Asia, and northwest Africa

species.name: Populus tremuloides
species.description: The species often propagates through its roots to form large clonal groves originating from a shared root system.

species.name: Prunus
species.description: This is the genus, lacking species identification.

species.name: Prunus × blireiana
species.description: It is a cross between the Japanese apricot (Prunus mume) and the purple-leaved plum (Prunus cerasifera var. 'Pissardii').

species.name: Prunus × yedoensis
species.native_region: Japan
species.description: A hybrid cherry of between Prunus speciosa (Oshima zakura) as father plant and Prunus pendula f. ascendens (Edo higan) as mother. It is a clone from a single tree and propagated by grafting to all over the world.

species.native_region: Europe, Anatolia, Maghreb, and Western Asia, from the British Isles south to Morocco and Tunisia, north to the Trondheimsfjord region in Norway and east to the Caucasus and northern Iran, with a small isolated population in the western Himalaya

species.name: Prunus cerasifera
species.native_region: Southeast Europe, Western Asia

species.name: Prunus cerasus

species.name: Prunus domestica
species.description:
Its hybrid parentage was believed to be Prunus spinosa and Prunus cerasifera. 

This is the most commonly grown plum at least in Europe, and most prunes (dried plums) are made from fruits of this species.

species.name: Prunus dulcis
species.native_region: Iran and surrounding countries

species.name: Prunus emarginata
species.description:
The bitter cherries are not edible by humans. However, they are eaten by some birds (especially cedar waxwing) and mammals, and deer and livestock forage on the leaves.

Indigenous peoples, most notably Kwakwaka'wakw, used other parts of the plant for medicinal purposes, such as poultices and bark infusions. Outer bark was harvested in strips from standing, living trees for wrapping implement joints, waterproofing, cordage, basket decoration; whistle reeds.

species.name: Prunus laurocerasus
species.native_region: regions bordering the Black Sea in southwestern Asia and southeastern Europe, from Albania and Bulgaria east through Turkey to the Caucasus Mountains and northern Iran
species.description: Prunus laurocerasus is a widely cultivated ornamental plant, used for planting in gardens and parks in temperate regions worldwide. It is often used for hedges, as a screening plant, and as a massed landscape plant.

species.name: Prunus lusitanica

species.description: It is used as an ornamental in many parts of the world for its striking coppery-red bark.

species.native_region: Japan

species.name: Prunus wadai
species.description: Hybrid of Prunus pseudocerasus (Chinese sour cherry) and Prunus subhirtella (Winter-flowering cherry).

species.name: Pseudotsuga menziesii
species.native_region: western North America
species.description:
Despite its common name, the Douglas-fir is not a true fir. It is also not a hemlock; the genus name Pseudotsuga means "false hemlock".

Many different Indigenous peoples used the bark, resin (pitch), and pine needles of Douglas-fir to make herbal treatments for various diseases. For the W̱SÁNEĆ people, Douglas-firs were the largest producer of pitch, which was a prized commodity for its many uses. Pitch was used in fire starting, patching open wounds as well as for sealing canoes. Bark for fuel would be cut from standing, living trees; self-pruned limbs from living trees used extensively for fuel; branches cut from living trees for pit-cooking, bedding, floor covering, and sweathouses.

Also used as a mixture with other plants for hair wash and skin wash during sweat bathing, needles as hair tonic (Nlaka’pamux, Okanagan); boughs used on floors, in sweathouse, for bereaved persons, used as tea during sweat bathing, cleansing agent (Nlaka’pamux, Okanagan, other groups); boughs used in ritual washing of twins, to construct puberty houses for girls, and in other ceremonial roles (Secwepemc, Okanagan, other Interior Plateau peoples) (Turner Bouchard, and Kennedy 1980; Turner, Thompson, et al. 1990).

Thick bark and wood were used as hot-burning fuels. Harpoon and spear shafts, dip net poles and hoops, arrow shafts, fish-barbecuing stakes. Bark slabs split off standing trees and used for shelter covering,
siding.

Douglas-fir seeds are an extremely important food source for small mammals such as moles, shrews, and chipmunks, which consume an estimated 65% of each annual seed crop.

The species is extensively used in forestry as a plantation tree for softwood timber. Douglas-fir has been commonly used as a Christmas tree since the 1920s.

The common name honors David Douglas, a Scottish botanist and collector who first reported the extraordinary nature and potential of the species. The specific epithet menziesii is after Archibald Menzies, a Scottish physician and rival naturalist to David Douglas. Menzies first documented the tree on Vancouver Island in 1791.

species.name: Pyrus calleryana
species.native_region: China and Vietnam

species.name: Quercus coccinea
species.native_region: the central and eastern United States
species.description: The scarlet oak can be mistaken for the pin oak, the black oak, or occasionally the red oak. On scarlet oak the sinuses between lobes are "C"-shaped in comparison to pin oak (Q. palustris), which has "U"-shaped sinuses and the acorns are half covered by a deep cap.

species.name: Quercus garryana
species.native_region: southern California to southwestern British Columbia
species.description:
Garry oak is the only native oak species in British Columbia, Washington, and northern Oregon.

Indigenous peoples burned the plants under the oaks throughout their range to maintain open prairie, to make hunting easier, and to allow the land to produce more food. The edible bulbs of camas and other species were the focus of the plant harvest. Camas was so important in their diet that families had their own plots of woodland where they owned the harvest. So important were these plants that the Victoria area was originally known as Camosun, or "place to gather camas."

The WSANEĆ peoples used the bark and leaves medicinally to help treat colds, stomach aches, cramps and even as a post-childbirth contraceptive. The bark can be infused to treat cuts, wounds, sore throats, and help treat diabetes while the inner bark was used to make dresses. Tannin, also found in the bark of Arbutus trees, was used to tan and cure hides.

Garry oak woodlands depend on disturbance to avoid being overtaken by Douglas-fir. Deliberate burning was widely practiced by the indigenous people of these areas. Fire perpetuated the grasslands that produced food sources such as camas, chocolate lily, bracken fern, and oak; and that provided grazing and easy hunting for deer and elk.

The eponymous Nicholas Garry was deputy governor of the Hudson's Bay Company, 1822–35.

species.name: Quercus palustris
species.native_region: eastern and central United States from Connecticut west to eastern Kansas, and south to Georgia, west to eastern Oklahoma and Kansas. It is also native in the extreme south of Ontario, Canada

species.name: Quercus robur
species.native_region: Most of Europe west of the Caucasus

species.name: Quercus rubra
species.native_region: North America, in the eastern and central United States and southeast and south-central Canada

species.name: Robinia pseudoacacia
species.native_region: eastern United States

species.name: Salix × sepulcralis 'Chrysocoma'
species.description: It is an artificial hybrid between S. alba 'Vitellina' and S. babylonica. The first parent provides the frost hardiness and the golden shoots and the second parent the strong weeping habit.

species.name: Salix babylonica
species.native_region: dry areas of northern China
species.description: The epithet babylonica in this Chinese species' scientific name (S. babylonica), as well as the related common names "Babylon willow" or "Babylon weeping willow", derive from a misunderstanding by Linnaeus that this willow was the tree described in the Bible in the opening of Psalm 137.

species.name: Salix nigra
species.native_region: eastern North America, from New Brunswick and southern Ontario west to Minnesota, and south to northern Florida and Texas

species.name: Salix scouleriana
species.native_region: western North America
species.description:
Scouler's willow protects the soil and helps return sites to forest cover following disturbances. When growing along streams, it helps protect the stream banks from erosion and shades the watercourse, thus maintaining cooler water temperatures. The cover provided is important for mammals and birds. The flowers provide pollen and nectar to honey bees in early spring.

Straits Salish peoples used bark and stems cut from living plants for cordage and netting which would regenerate in following years.

The Secwepemc people of British Columbia used the wood for smoking fish, drying meat, and constructing fishing weirs, the inner bark for lashing, sowing, cordage, and headbands, and decoctions of twigs for treating pimples, body odor, and diaper rash.

species.name: Salix sitchensis
species.native_region: northwestern North America from Alaska to northern California to Montana

species.name: Sequoiadendron giganteum
species.native_region: groves on the western slopes of the Sierra Nevada Mountains of California
species.description:
Giant sequoia specimens are the most massive trees on Earth. 

The etymology of the genus name is in honor of Sequoyah (1767–1843), a polymath of the Cherokee Nation who was the inventor of the Cherokee syllabary.

Giant sequoias are in many ways adapted to forest fires. Their bark is unusually fire resistant, and their cones will normally open immediately after a fire.

species.name: Sorbus aucuparia
species.native_region: most of Europe and parts of Asia, as well as northern Africa

species.name: Sorbus intermedia
species.native_region: southern Sweden, with scattered occurrences in easternmost Denmark (Bornholm), the far southwest of Finland, Estonia, Latvia and northern Poland

species.name: Stewartia pseudocamellia
species.native_region: Japan (southern Honshū, Kyūshū, Shikoku) and Korea
species.description: The Latin specific epithet pseudocamellia references the flower’s resemblance to the related camellia.

species.name: Taxodium distichum
species.native_region: the southeastern United States
species.description: Bald cypress trees are deciduous (not evergreen) and when growing in swamps have a peculiarity of growth called cypress knees - woody projections from the root system project above the ground or water. It is still unknown what purpose these serve.

species.name: Taxus baccata
species.native_region: western, central and southern Europe, northwest Africa, northern Iran and southwest Asia

species.name: Taxus brevifolia
species.native_region: Pacific Northwest of North America
species.description:
Used by indigenous peoples for implement handles, digging sticks, clubs, mallets, wedges, bows, snowshoes, gambling disks, blanket pins, pegs, fishhooks (bent) and halibut fishing gear.

Tree would be “talked to” before a piece was cut for bows or other tools (Kwakwaka’wakw); branches used for ritual scrubbing and purification (Ditidaht, Nlaka’pamux, and others) (Turner, Thomas, et al. 1983, 1990).

species.name: Thuja occidentalis
species.native_region: eastern Canada and much of the north, central and upper Northeastern United States

species.name: Thuja plicata
species.native_region: western North America
species.description:
Western redcedar is also known as the giant arborvitae, by comparison with arborvitae for its close relative Thuja occidentalis. Arborvitae comes from the Latin for "tree of life"; coincidentally, indigenous peoples of the West coast also address the species as "long life maker". Western redcedar is a member of the cypress family and not a true cedar of the genus Cedrus.

Western red cedar has an extensive history of use by Indigenous peoples. Some northwest coast tribes refer to themselves as "people of the redcedar" because of their extensive dependence on the tree for basic materials. The wood has been used for constructing housing and totem poles, and crafted into many objects, including masks, utensils, boxes, boards, instruments, canoes, vessels, houses, and ceremonial objects. Western Red Cedar is also associated with a long tradition of curing and cooking fish over the open fire. Roots and bark are used for baskets, bowls, ropes, clothing, blankets, and rings.

species.name: Thujopsis dolabrata
species.native_region: Japan
species.description: The hiba arborvitae / asunaro is a valued ornamental tree both in its native Japan, where it is commonly planted around temples as well as in gardens, and also in Europe and North America.

species.name: Tilia americana
species.native_region: eastern North America, from southeast Manitoba east to New Brunswick, southwest to northeast Oklahoma, southeast to South Carolina, and west along the Niobrara River to Cherry County, Nebraska
species.description: Its flowers provide abundant nectar for insects. The seeds are eaten by chipmunks, mice, and squirrels. Rabbits and voles eat the bark, sometimes girdling young trees.

species.name: Tilia cordata
species.native_region: from Britain through mainland Europe to the Caucasus and western Asia
species.description: Tilia cordata is widely grown as an ornamental tree. It was much planted to form avenues in 17th and early 18th century landscape planning.

species.name: Torreya californica
species.native_region: the Pacific Coast Ranges and the foothills of the Sierra Nevada
species.description: California nutmeg is not closely related to true nutmeg. The wood is sometimes used in making Go game boards, as a cheaper substitute for the prized kaya (Torreya nucifera) of Japan and Southeast Asia.

species.name: Tsuga heterophylla
species.description:
Western hemlock is a very shade-tolerant tree; among associated species in the Pacific Northwest, it is matched or exceeded in shade tolerance only by Pacific yew and Pacific silver fir. Young plants typically grow up under the canopy of other conifers such as Sitka spruce or Douglas-fir, where they can persist for decades waiting to exploit a gap in the canopy. They eventually replace these conifers, which are relatively shade-intolerant, in climax forest. However, storms and wildfires will create larger openings in the forest where these other species can then regenerate.

Western hemlock forms ectomycorrhizal associations with some well-known edible fungi such as chanterelles. It is capable of associating with wood-decay fungi in addition to soil fungi; this enables its seedlings to survive on rotting stumps and logs.

Boughs were used as ritual scrubbers to protect girls at puberty, hunters (Kwakwaka’wakw, Hesquiaht/Nuu-chah-nulth, Ditidaht, Makah, Nlaka’pamux); decoction of branches drunk for ritual purification and used as disinfecting fumigant for houses (Nlaka’pamux) (Boas 1930; Gill 1983; Turner and Bell 1973; Turner and Efrat 1982; Turner, Thompson, et al. 1990). Knots for bentwood fishhooks; wood for harpoon shafts, fish weir stakes, arrow points, paddles. Boughs for lining acorn-leaching pits, reinforcing fish weirs,
capturing herring eggs. 

The Ditidaht name qw’itłqapt, for western hemlock, means “fire goes out/no fire-tree/plant” because it is considered a poor-burning wood, although it is sometimes used for banking a fire overnight because it will smoulder without putting out much heat.

The sap or pitch is medicinal, used as a poultice to heal wounds and burns, as well as mixed with fat to form an aromatic salve that is useful as a chest rub for colds, to massage sore muscles, and to protect against sunburn.

Harvesting: Partial harvesting of edible cambium and inner bark. Rectangular pieces cut from living trees.            Harvesting pitch or gum from living trees for material or medicinal purposes. Collected from natural or human-made wounds in trees or from pitch blisters. The pitch was variously chewed for pleasure, used as waterproofing or adhesive for implements and containers, or prepared for medicinal use. Bark harvested for food (inner bark) from standing, living trees; branches and sapling trunks cut for herring egg harvesting, lining acorn-leaching pits, and reinforcing weirs; poles cut for weirs and twisting eelgrass (general, Northwest Coast)

species.native_region: Southern Europe
